Years 11–13 Health and
Physical Education

Learning expectations
Through the Health and Physical Education learning area, students develop the knowledge, skills,
and critical capabilities needed to understand and strengthen health, well-being, physical activity,
relationships with place, participation, and performance. They are taught how to evaluate evidence,
make informed decisions, manage risk in changing environments, participate confidently, and
design responses that support safe, inclusive, equitable, and meaningful experiences.

The learning area supports students to evaluate evidence, make informed decisions, participate
confidently, and design responses that support safe, inclusive, equitable, and meaningful
experiences in relation to people, communities, and places.


Key features of the refreshed learning area
•     Stronger emphasis on evidence, data, critical health literacy, ethical decision-making, inclusion,
      social justice, equity, and contemporary health and physical activity issues.
•     Clear progression from Year 11 Physical Education to the more specialised Years 12–13
      Physical Education pathway.
•     Explicit knowledge and practices clarify the concepts, theories, terminology, skills, strategies,
      and applications students are to be taught.
•     Greater disciplinary depth in anatomy, biomechanics, physiology, skill learning, coaching,
      psychology, leadership, participation, and the social and cultural contexts of physical activity.
•     Practical experiences are connected explicitly to disciplinary concepts, analysis, reflection,
      adaptation, and evidence-informed decision-making.
•     Disciplinary writing supports students to communicate increasingly sophisticated explanations,
      analyses, evaluations, judgements, and recommendations.


Subjects
Subjects within the Health and Physical Education Learning Area are:

•     Years 11–13 Health Studies
•     Year 11 Physical Education
•     Years 12–13 Physical Education
•     Years 12–13 Outdoor Education. 1

Learning and pathways

Years 11–13 Health Studies
Students are taught how personal, social, cultural, economic, technological, and systemic factors
influence individual and community health and well-being. They study relationships, mental health,
nutrition, health access, digital environments, disease, discrimination, and healthy communities.
Students use health concepts, models, data, evidence, and ethical reasoning to analyse health
issues and evaluate information, policies, services, and interventions.

Strands

Years 11–13 Health Studies is organised into four strands:

•   Relationships and Society
•   Mental Health and Well-being
•   Physical Health
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Health Studies provides foundations for further learning and pathways in health
sciences, public and community health, education, social and community services, psychology,
policy, technology, environmental health, research, and public service roles.

Year 11 Physical Education
Students are taught how movement is produced, learned, adapted, and experienced. They apply
knowledge of anatomy, biomechanics, physiology, skill learning, psychology, leadership, and
sociocultural influences to analyse participation, performance, and well-being. Students refine
movement and tactical responses and examine how physical activity connects with culture,
identity, place, and changing social norms.

Strands

Year 11 Physical Education is organised into five strands:

•   The Moving Body
•   Capability and Connection
•   Leadership and the Psychology of Movement
•   Sport and Physical Activity Culture
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Year 11 Physical Education provides foundations for Years 12–13 Physical Education and
pathways in sport and exercise sciences, coaching, leadership, fitness, education, health and
physical activity promotion, community recreation, and sport performance.

Years 12–13 Physical Education
Students are taught to integrate knowledge of anatomy, biomechanics, physiology, skill learning,
coaching, sport psychology, leadership, participation, and the social and cultural contexts of
physical activity. They analyse complex physical activity situations and design, adapt, and evaluate
training, coaching, leadership, and participation responses using practical experience and
disciplinary evidence.

Strands

Years 12–13 Physical Education is organised into five strands:

•   The Moving Body
•   Capability and Connection
•   Leadership and the Psychology of Movement
•   Systems and Social Structures
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Physical Education provides foundations for pathways in sport and exercise science,
physical education, coaching, leadership, fitness, health and physical activity promotion,
community recreation, sport management, and performance.


Connections to other learning areas
The Health and Physical Education learning area connects strongly with:

•   Science through anatomy, biomechanics, physiology, nutrition, disease, epidemiology, and the
    interpretation of scientific evidence
•   Social Sciences through identity, culture, communities, social justice, equity, policy, media,
    economics, power, and social systems
•   Technology through health technologies, wearable devices, adaptive equipment, digital
    platforms, artificial intelligence (AI), data privacy, and emerging technologies
•   Mathematics and Statistics through data interpretation, measurement, epidemiological
    measures, participation patterns, performance data, training variables, and risk.
•   All learning areas through disciplinary writing, critical thinking, ethical reasoning, collaboration,
    evidence-based communication, and evaluation of information and claims.


How to design a programme
•   Teachers should develop an overview of the full teaching sequence to ensure all compulsory
    knowledge and practices are addressed across the year.
•   Programmes should provide deliberate coverage, coherence, and progression, recognising that
    strands and elements are interconnected and can be taught in purposeful combinations.

•   The teaching sequence supports non-linear programme design. Teachers may integrate
    complementary statements or treat sub-elements as discrete areas of learning where
    appropriate.
•   Examples identified by ‘e.g.’ are guidance only. Teachers may select contexts that meet the
    intended learning and reflect local environments, iwi and hapū connections, student interests,
    community contexts, and teacher expertise.
•   Practical experiences, investigations, data, case material, and health or physical activity
    contexts should enable students to apply knowledge and demonstrate disciplinary practices.
•   Disciplinary writing should be integrated across the programme through regular opportunities to
    explain concepts, interpret evidence, analyse issues, evaluate responses, and justify
    conclusions and recommendations.
